title: Kabir's mother weeps
hook: in one hymn his mother cries that her son sings of the Lord instead of weaving (Gujri, Kabir)
tomorrow: The elephant that would not charge

segments.voice: Yesterday, warp and weft, and your line, woven. Did you follow one thread until it slipped under another? Today the loom goes quiet, and someone notices. Day seven hundred fifty.

The loom has stopped. In a small house in Kashi there's no clack of the shuttle today, and no cloth to take to market. There are children to feed. And in the next room, a woman is crying quietly, the kind of crying that tries not to be heard. Her son, the weaver, is singing again. Not working. Singing about the Lord. The remarkable thing is who tells us this scene. It's Kabir himself, in a hymn that sits in the Guru Granth Sahib. He sets his own mother's tears inside his song. Today: Kabir's mother weeps.
screen: `THE LOOM HAS STOPPED.` → `CHILDREN TO FEED.` → `HIS MOTHER, CRYING.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gujri. It opens with her: Kabir's mother sobs and sobs, and asks the Lord how these children will live. Kabir, she says, has given up weaving and spinning, and written the Lord's name on his body. Stop there a moment. She isn't a villain in this story. She's doing the sums. A weaver who doesn't weave has no cloth, and no cloth means no food. It is the arithmetic of anyone lying awake over rent. Kabir doesn't mock her for it. He puts her tears first, before his own answer, so her side is heard first. Then he speaks. As long as he's passing thread through the bobbin, he says, he forgets the Lord he loves. The work keeps pulling his mind away. And the hymn ends with Kabir turning to her, gently: listen, my mother, the one Lord is the giver, for me and for these children too. That's the whole answer. Not, stop worrying. Not, you don't understand. Just: the same Giver holds all of us. Sikh readers hold this hymn with care. The Gurus taught honest work as part of the path, so it isn't read as permission to quit your job. It's read as a picture of a heart so full of the Name that the loom couldn't hold it, and of a son who still answers his mother tenderly. Today's line comes out of that answer. Mother, he's weaving love. The cloth has changed, and the thread is still running.
screen: `RAAG GUJRI: HER TEARS COME FIRST.` · `SHE'S DOING THE SUMS.` · `THE BOBBIN PULLS HIS MIND AWAY.` · `ONE GIVER, FOR ALL OF US.` · then, large: `MOTHER, HE'S WEAVING LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive a worried parent. Or a grandparent, or whoever worried over you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one time their worry came out sideways: a sharp word, a nagging question, a fear about your choices. Now look underneath it, the way Kabir did. What were they counting? Food, safety, your future? Let the worry be what it was, sums done late at night. If forgiving feels too big today, just soften toward them by one notch. If you pray, you can hold their name with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Kabir's mother weeps. A hymn in Raag Gujri where Kabir sets his mother's tears first, and answers her: one Lord is the giver for us all.
Your line: mother, he's weaving love. Today, when someone worries at you, hear the sums underneath before you answer, and answer gently. Day seven hundred fifty.

notes: Hymn paraphrased throughout; confirm Ang 524 and the renderings ('sobs and sobs', 'written the Lord's name on his body', 'as long as he passes thread through the bobbin he forgets the Lord', 'the one Lord is the giver for me and these children').
'The Gurus taught honest work as part of the path' (kirat karni): general teaching, no specific text cited; confirm framing that the hymn is not read as permission to quit work.
The carry 'mother, he's weaving love' is the index line; it shifts voice from Kabir ('me') to a third person. Kept exactly; Keeper may want the index reworded.
Practice asks to 'forgive a worried parent'; softened with an option for listeners whose parents were harder than worried. Confirm tone.
